past_medical_history: No prior neuromuscular or autoimmune disease

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x4. Normal language and cognition.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, left greater than right — levator excursion left 5mm, right 8mm. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze complete in left eye at 40 seconds. Horizontal diplopia on rightward gaze. Mild limitation of right eye adduction. Pupils equal, 3mm, reactive. No proptosis. Bilateral mild facial weakness.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity weakness: deltoids 4/5 bilaterally, worse on left. Proximal lower extremity: hip flexors 4+/5. Distal strength 5/5. Neck flexors 4/5. Classic fatigability: deltoid strength drops from 4 to 3/5 after 10 repetitions.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal casual. Waddling on prolonged walking.
neurological_exam.additional: Dysarthria after 3 minutes sustained speech. Mild dysphagia — reports difficulty with pills. NIF -58 cmH2O (borderline). No respiratory distress. No stridor.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and arm fatigue worse at end of day over 3 months
patient.history_present_illness: A 34-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressive bilateral ptosis, horizontal diplopia, and proximal arm weakness. She first noticed bilateral eyelid drooping approximately 3 months ago, initially only in the evenings. Over time, the ptosis became present throughout the day and progressively worsened, with the left eye more severely affected than the right. She began experiencing double vision when looking to the right, which was intermittent initially but became more frequent. She noticed that her arms became weak and fatigued when blow-drying her hair or reaching for overhead items — she could not maintain her arms elevated for more than 60 seconds. She began having difficulty chewing tough meats by the end of a meal, requiring rest breaks. Her speech became slurred and nasal after prolonged conversation, particularly noticeable in the evenings during dinner. She works as a nurse and noticed she had increasing difficulty performing overhead tasks and her handwriting was becoming affected. She denies any sensory symptoms, no headache, no visual acuity changes, no neck pain, no back pain, no bladder or bowel dysfunction. Her symptoms consistently worsen throughout the day and are significantly better in the morning after sleep. She had a brief visit to urgent care 6 weeks ago where she was told the ptosis was 'stress-related' and given a recommendation to reduce work hours. She has had no recent viral illnesses, no vaccinations, and no new medications. She is otherwise completely healthy. Her mother and aunts have no neuromuscular disease. The classic diurnal variation and fatigability pattern are well-documented on this admission.

specialized_test.test_type: Repetitive Nerve Stimulation, EMG, and NCS

findings.significance: Pattern of post-exercise repair with subsequent exhaustion

findings.result: 2 mg IV test dose — improvement in ptosis within 30 seconds (ptosis reduced from complete to partial); 8 mg IV — complete resolution of ptosis and diplopia for 5 minutes
findings.significance: Positive pharmacological response — prompt improvement in ptosis and diplopia following edrophonium administration

findings.result: Normal motor and sensory — normal baseline CMAP amplitudes
findings.significance: Normal motor and sensory conduction; normal baseline CMAP amplitudes

specialized_test.impression: Clearly abnormal RNS with 16–22% decremental responses across multiple muscle groups. Positive edrophonium (Tensilon) test with prompt reversal of ptosis and diplopia. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

labs.interpretation: Anti-AChR binding antibody markedly elevated at 12.4 nmol/L (reference <0.5 nmol/L). Anti-AChR blocking and modulating antibodies also elevated. Anti-MuSK antibody negative. Anti-striated muscle (anti-titin) antibody negative. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in a subset of patients with neuromuscular junction disorders; elevated results are associated with autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease. Clinical correlation recommended.
abnormal_values_summary: Anti-AChR binding 12.4 nmol/L (markedly elevated; ref <0.5 nmol/L)

findings.density: Heterogeneous soft tissue density with areas of low attenuation
findings.description: Large anterior mediastinal mass. Lobulated borders. Displaces adjacent mediastinal structures but no clear invasion. Contains areas of necrosis or cystic degeneration.

ct.impression: Large anterior mediastinal mass measuring 4.2 x 3.8 cm with heterogeneous soft tissue density and areas of internal low attenuation. Lobulated margins. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Fat planes with adjacent great vessels appear preserved. No pleural effusion. Lungs clear. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.significance: Severely increased jitter — most abnormal possible range
Very high blocking — severe NMJ failure

output.impression: Severely abnormal SFEMG with markedly increased jitter (mean MCD 88 µs) and high blocking rate (90%). Findings are consistent with severe neuromuscular transmission failure. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.proposed: IVIG 2g/kg over 5 days pre-operatively for thymectomy preparation in markedly positive AChR-MG
interactions: IVIG + oral contraceptive: IVIG does not significantly affect OCP efficacy
IVIG + anti-AChR antibodies: IVIG provides immunomodulation reducing AChR antibody titers over 2-4 weeks
contraindications: Check IgA levels before IVIG — IgA deficiency can cause anaphylaxis with IVIG
Renal function check before IVIG (high-volume fluid load)
warnings: IVIG for pre-operative optimization — onset 2-5 days; peak effect 2-4 weeks
Pre-medicate with diphenhydramine and acetaminophen to prevent infusion reactions
output.formulary_status: IVIG: formulary (requires prior authorization; hospitalization indication justifies)
alternatives: Plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) 5 sessions over 10 days — faster onset than IVIG; useful when thymectomy cannot wait 2-4 weeks

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb-III), AChR antibody-positive, with large thymoma (4.2 cm anterior mediastinal mass)

differential.key_features: Imaging cannot definitively distinguish; tissue diagnosis (surgical resection) required.
Markedly elevated AChR titers and normal baseline CMAPs exclude LEMS.
No proptosis or lid retraction; fatigable rather than restrictive.
Markedly elevated AChR antibodies and RNS decrement establish organic pathology.
Acute 3-month onset and fatigable pattern incompatible with CPEO.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Improvement of ptosis after 2 minutes of cooling supports MG

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Confirm markedly positive AChR antibodies (binding 8.7 nmol/L)
CT chest — large 4.2 cm anterior mediastinal mass; urgent thoracic surgery referral
Pre-thymectomy MG optimization: pyridostigmine + IVIG or PLEX bridge
Single-fiber EMG if diagnostic uncertainty (here serology and RNS already conclusive)
Consider non-hormonal contraception during high-dose immunosuppression
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Anti-titin or anti-RyR antibodies in an MG patient strongly predict thymoma — CT chest is mandatory and surgical referral is non-negotiable.
Markedly positive AChR titer (8.7 nmol/L) + 15-24% RNS decrement = classic generalized MG; SFEMG is recommended but no longer mandatory for diagnosis.
Large thymoma (>3 cm) is a surgical priority; thymectomy improves both MG and oncologic outcomes.
